title: What plumbers charge in regional NSW
description: Indicative callout fees of $70 to $150, hourly rates, after hours loading, and the eight things a plumbing quote should itemise.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Most people ring three plumbers, get three different numbers, and have no way to judge which one is fair. What follows is an indicative range for domestic plumbing in regional New South Wales, drawn from what small trade businesses in the Riverina, the Murray and the Central West commonly quote. It is not a price list. No plumber is bound by it. Use it as a sanity check on the quote in front of you.

## The callout fee

Almost every plumber charges to turn up. In regional NSW the callout fee usually sits in an indicative range of $70 to $150 including GST for a weekday job inside a town. Some businesses roll the first 30 minutes of labour into that figure. Some do not. That one question decides whether a $90 callout is cheap or dear.

Past the town boundary the fee grows. A plumber based in Albury quoting a job at Holbrook is looking at about 80 kilometres each way, so expect travel on top, billed either per kilometre or as a flat zone fee. Ask where the zone boundary sits before you book. Farm sheds and lifestyle blocks past the last sealed road attract the surcharges nobody mentions on the phone.

## Hourly rates

For general domestic work the indicative weekday rate across regional NSW runs about $90 to $150 an hour including GST. Wagga Wagga, Albury and Orange sit at the top of that band because new housing and commercial work compete for the same trades. Smaller towns can be cheaper by the hour and dearer overall, because travel eats the difference.

Most plumbers bill in 15 or 30 minute increments after a minimum charge. A one hour minimum is normal. A two hour minimum for a five minute tap washer is not, and it is worth raising before the ute leaves the depot. Apprentice time should be billed at a lower rate than the licence holder standing next to them.

## After hours loading

After hours means different things to different businesses. For some it starts at 5pm, for others at 4.30pm or on the Saturday morning. The common structure in regional NSW is a higher callout fee plus a loaded hourly rate, with the loading landing in an indicative range of 1.5 to 2 times the weekday rate. Public holidays commonly run at double, sometimes more, and often carry a minimum of two hours.

That matters more on the border than anywhere else, because a day that is an ordinary Tuesday in Albury can be a gazetted holiday in Wodonga. We set out which days differ in [the NSW and Victorian public holidays guide](/guides/public-holidays-nsw-vs-vic/).

A real emergency is a burst pipe, a gas leak, sewage backing up into the house, or no water at all. A dripping tap on a Sunday is not, and paying emergency rates for it is a choice.

## Indicative ranges for common jobs

These are ranges for straightforward domestic work in a regional town, including GST, parts and labour, on an accessible job. Old houses, tight roof spaces, asbestos sheeting and long pipe runs push everything up.

| Job | Indicative range |
| --- | --- |
| Tap washer or cartridge replaced | $90 to $220 |
| Blocked drain cleared with a machine | $200 to $450 |
| Drain jetting with camera inspection | $400 to $900 |
| Electric storage hot water unit replaced | $1,300 to $2,600 |
| Continuous flow gas unit replaced | $1,800 to $3,800 |
| Toilet suite replaced | $500 to $1,100 |
| Accessible burst pipe repaired | $250 to $600 |
| Gas appliance connected and tested | $200 to $500 |

Hot water is the job most often quoted badly. The unit itself is maybe half the cost. The rest is the tempering valve, the new isolation valve, the tray and drain if it sits inside, disposal of the old unit, and an electrician if the circuit needs work. A quote that names only the unit price is not a quote.

## What a quote should itemise

1. The callout fee, and whether any labour is included in it.
2. The hourly rate, the billing increment, and the minimum charge.
3. The after hours or weekend rate, written down, not described on the phone.
4. Travel, either as a kilometre rate or a named zone fee.
5. Parts, listed by item, so you can see what is being installed.
6. Rubbish removal and disposal of the old unit.
7. The warranty on labour, and the manufacturer warranty on parts, as separate figures.
8. The licence number and the business name and ABN the money is going to.

If the quote is a single number with no breakdown, ask for the breakdown. A plumber who will not put the callout fee in writing will not put anything else in writing either.

## Licensing and written contracts

Plumbing, draining and gasfitting all need a licence from NSW Fair Trading, and the authorisations are separate. A plumber licensed for water and sanitary work is not automatically allowed to touch gas. The licence number belongs on the quote and on the invoice. You can put it through our [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/), and the step by step is in [how to check a tradie licence](/guides/how-to-check-a-tradie-licence/).

Residential work above a threshold in the low thousands of dollars needs a written contract under the Home Building Act, and larger jobs also need home building compensation cover taken out by the contractor. The thresholds are set in legislation and have moved over the years, so confirm the current figures with NSW Fair Trading rather than trusting a number from a forum post. The point stands regardless of the exact dollar line. Anything beyond a service call should be in writing before work starts.

## Comparing quotes without getting burnt

Get the quotes on the same scope. Three prices for three different jobs tell you nothing. Write down what you want done, send the same words to each business, and ask each to price that scope.

Be suspicious of a quote that is far below the others. It usually means something has been left out, most often the making good, the disposal, or the compliance work that turns a repair into a legal installation. Be equally suspicious of a fixed price given over the phone for a drain nobody has looked at.

Ask when they can start and hold them to it. In harvest and in the fortnight after a cold snap, response times across the Riverina blow out badly, and the business that answers the phone is not always the business that turns up.

Start with the listings for [plumbers in Albury](/nsw/albury/plumbers/) or [plumbers in Wagga Wagga](/nsw/wagga-wagga/plumbers/), or browse the [plumbers category](/categories/plumbers/) for other towns.

faqs.q: Is a callout fee refundable if the plumber cannot fix the problem?
faqs.a: Usually not. The callout fee pays for travel and time on site, not for a successful repair. Some businesses credit it against the job if you go ahead with the quoted work, so ask before you book. If a plumber diagnoses the fault and quotes the fix, that is the callout fee doing its job.

faqs.q: What is a fair after hours rate in regional NSW?
faqs.a: An indicative loading of 1.5 to 2 times the weekday rate is normal after hours, with a higher callout fee on top. Public holidays commonly run at double or more with a two hour minimum. The rate should be stated before the plumber leaves, not written on the invoice afterwards.

faqs.q: Do I need a written quote for a small plumbing job?
faqs.a: You do not legally need one for a minor service call, but get the callout fee and hourly rate in a text message anyway. Written contracts become a legal requirement for residential work above a threshold set under the Home Building Act, and that threshold is easy to cross once you add a hot water unit or bathroom work. Confirm the current figure with NSW Fair Trading.

faqs.q: Why did the plumber charge travel when the job was only 20 minutes away?
faqs.a: Travel time is the biggest hidden cost in regional work. Twenty minutes each way is 40 minutes the business cannot bill to anyone else, so most price it as a zone fee or a kilometre rate outside their base town. Ask where the free zone ends when you first call.

faqs.q: Can a plumber do the gas work as well?
faqs.a: Only if they hold a gasfitting authorisation on their NSW licence. Plumbing, draining and gasfitting are separate authorisations and plenty of licensed plumbers hold only some of them. Check the licence number against the register before gas work starts.

title: What electricians charge in regional Victoria
description: Indicative hourly rates of $85 to $150, callout fees, after hours loading, and why a Certificate of Electrical Safety matters.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Electrical pricing in country Victoria is easier to compare than plumbing, because most jobs are repeatable. A power point is a power point. What moves the number is travel, the age of the switchboard, and whether the job needs an inspection before it can be signed off. The ranges below are indicative for domestic work in regional Victoria and are not quoted prices.

## Callout fees and minimum charges

Most regional Victorian electricians charge a callout fee in an indicative range of $70 to $140 including GST, or fold it into a one hour minimum. A common structure in Wodonga, Wangaratta and Shepparton is a first hour charge that covers arrival and the first block of work, then time billed in 15 minute steps.

The further out you are, the more the structure changes. Businesses working the Upper Murray and the alpine towns often price by the half day, because a run from Wodonga to Corryong is about 120 kilometres and there is no second job nearby to share the trip with. That is not a rip off. It is the only way the day pays.

## Hourly rates

The indicative weekday rate for a licensed electrician in regional Victoria runs about $85 to $150 an hour including GST. Bendigo, Ballarat, Geelong and the Wodonga corridor sit near the top. Apprentice hours should be billed lower, and a two person crew should be quoted as two rates, not one mystery figure.

After hours work commonly runs at 1.5 to 2 times the weekday rate. Public holidays sit higher again, often at double with a minimum of two or three hours. Victoria has more gazetted holidays than New South Wales, including the Friday before the AFL Grand Final and Melbourne Cup Day, which is why an emergency callout on those days costs more than the same job across the river. The detail is in [the public holidays comparison](/guides/public-holidays-nsw-vs-vic/).

## Indicative ranges for common jobs

Supplied and installed, including GST, on a house with a switchboard that is not a disaster.

| Job | Indicative range |
| --- | --- |
| Extra power point on an existing circuit | $150 to $320 |
| Replace a light fitting | $110 to $250 |
| Downlights, per light in an existing ceiling | $80 to $160 |
| Safety switch added to the board | $180 to $400 |
| Full switchboard upgrade | $1,000 to $2,800 |
| Hard wired smoke alarm replaced | $150 to $400 |
| Ceiling fan installed where wiring exists | $200 to $450 |
| Single phase EV charger installed | $1,200 to $2,600 |

Switchboard upgrades are the job with the widest spread, and for good reason. A 1970s board with rewireable fuses, a ceramic main switch and cotton covered wiring behind it is a different job to a 2005 board that needs two more circuit breakers. No honest electrician quotes that one sight unseen.

## Country jobs that cost more than people expect

Rural properties add work that town jobs do not have. A supply run from the meter box to a shed 90 metres away needs cable sized for the voltage drop, and the cable is usually the biggest line on the quote. Pump circuits, irrigation controls and dairy sheds need weatherproof gear and RCD protection. Properties on single wire earth return supply have real limits on what can be connected, and a good sparky will tell you that before you buy the three phase welder.

Storm work is its own category. After a front comes through the north east, every electrician between Bright and Yarrawonga is booked, and the first question is always whether the damage is on your side of the point of supply or the distributor's side. If the service cable to the house is down, that is a call to the distributor, not to a private contractor.

## Certificates and who signs off

This is the part that separates Victoria from New South Wales. Electrical work in Victoria is regulated by Energy Safe Victoria. The person doing the work holds an electrical licence, and the business contracting for the work should be a Registered Electrical Contractor.

When the work is finished you should receive a Certificate of Electrical Safety. For prescribed work, which covers the higher risk categories such as switchboard and mains work, the certificate also requires inspection by a licensed electrical inspector before it is issued. You do not arrange that inspector. The contractor does, and the cost belongs in the quote.

Keep the certificate. It is what an insurer asks for after a fire, what a conveyancer asks for at sale, and the only simple proof that the work was done by someone entitled to do it. If a job that clearly needs one produces no certificate, that is the loudest warning sign in the trade.

You can look up an electrical contractor through our [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/), and the walkthrough for both states is in [how to check a tradie licence](/guides/how-to-check-a-tradie-licence/).

## What the quote should say

A usable electrical quote names the scope job by job, not as a lump. It states the hourly rate and the minimum charge, lists the major materials, says who pays for the electrical inspector on prescribed work, and confirms that a Certificate of Electrical Safety will be issued. It carries the contractor registration number and the ABN.

On larger jobs, ask about the make of the switchgear. There is a real price difference between brands, and a cheap quote sometimes means budget breakers in a board you will keep for 25 years.

Ask about clean up and patching too. Chasing walls for new cabling leaves damage, and most electricians make good to a rough finish, not a painted one. Knowing who patches and who paints avoids the argument later.

## Getting quotes that compare

Write the scope once and send the same words to three businesses. Ask each of them for the callout fee, the hourly rate, the after hours rate and the expected attendance window. Then ask when they could start, because in country Victoria availability is often worth more than a $60 difference in the quote.

Start with [electricians in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/electricians/) or [electricians in Wangaratta](/vic/wangaratta/electricians/), or open the [electricians category](/categories/electricians/) to find a town further out.

faqs.q: What is a Certificate of Electrical Safety and do I need one?
faqs.a: It is the document a Victorian electrical contractor issues to certify the work complies with the wiring rules. You should receive one for electrical installation work, and for prescribed work it is issued after a licensed electrical inspector has checked the job. Keep it with your property records, because insurers and conveyancers ask for it.

faqs.q: Who pays for the electrical inspector on prescribed work?
faqs.a: The contractor arranges the inspector and the cost should be included in their quote. You do not book the inspector yourself. If a quote for switchboard or mains work does not mention inspection, ask where that cost sits before you accept it.

faqs.q: Are electricians licensed by the Victorian Building Authority?
faqs.a: No. Electrical licensing and contractor registration in Victoria sit with Energy Safe Victoria. The Victorian Building Authority handles builders and plumbers. That split catches people out when they search the wrong register and find nothing.

faqs.q: Why is a switchboard upgrade quoted as a range?
faqs.a: Because nobody knows what is behind the panel until it comes off. Old rewireable fuses, undersized mains, missing earthing and deteriorated cabling all change the job. A fair electrician quotes a range, explains what would push it to the top of that range, and confirms the price once the board is open.

faqs.q: Can a NSW licensed electrician work in Victoria?
faqs.a: Often yes, under mutual recognition arrangements, but the work still has to meet Victorian rules including the Certificate of Electrical Safety and inspection requirements. The business also needs to be entitled to contract for the work in Victoria. Check the detail in our guide to NSW and Victorian licence rules.

title: How a NSW trade licence works in Victoria, and back again
description: Mutual recognition, Automatic Mutual Recognition, and the five things to check before you hire across the NSW and Victorian border.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
A licence is a piece of state law. New South Wales and Victoria each run their own system, with their own classes, their own conditions and their own registers. That is why the same plumber can be fully licensed on one side of the Murray and unlicensed on the other unless something bridges the gap.

Two things bridge the gap. Both are worth understanding before you hire.

## Mutual recognition, the old path

Mutual recognition has existed since the early 1990s under Commonwealth and state legislation. It lets a person licensed in one state apply for the equivalent licence in another state without repeating the training or the exams. The second regulator can attach conditions so the licence lines up with local law, and there is an application and a fee.

The result is a real second licence. A Wodonga plumber who takes this path holds a Victorian licence and a New South Wales licence, appears on both registers, and can be checked on both. For a business that works both sides of the border every week, this is still the cleanest arrangement.

## Automatic Mutual Recognition, the newer path

Automatic Mutual Recognition, usually shortened to AMR, started in 2021. The idea is that a person with a licence in their home state can work in another participating state without applying for a second licence at all. They notify the second state's regulator where required, they carry their home state licence, and they work under the second state's rules.

The important word is participating. AMR does not cover every occupation in every state. Some occupations are excluded, some were deferred by a state, and some carry extra notification requirements. The scope has shifted since it began and it can shift again. Do not assume it covers the trade you are hiring. Check the current position on the regulator's site for the state where the work will happen.

AMR also does not change the rules of the job. It changes who has to hold what paperwork. Everything else, meaning the standards, the certificates, the notifications and the insurance, follows the state where the work is done.

## What does not travel across the border

This is where people come unstuck.

- **Compliance paperwork.** Electrical work done in Victoria needs a Victorian Certificate of Electrical Safety, whoever the electrician is. Plumbing work done in Victoria needs a Victorian compliance certificate for the classes that require one. Neither is replaced by a New South Wales equivalent.
- **Warranty insurance.** Residential building work above a threshold needs home building compensation cover in New South Wales and domestic building insurance in Victoria. They are different products under different schemes. A builder covered in one state is not covered in the other.
- **Business entitlement.** A licence held by an individual is not the same as the entitlement of the company to contract for work. In Victoria an electrical business contracting for work should be a Registered Electrical Contractor. In New South Wales the business needs a contractor licence in its own name.
- **Where you complain.** A dispute about work done in New South Wales goes to NSW Fair Trading and then to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal. A dispute about work done in Victoria goes to Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Victorian Building Authority and then to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. The address of the tradie does not decide this. The address of the job does.

## The regulators, and which one you want

New South Wales keeps most trade licensing with NSW Fair Trading, including builders, plumbers, drainers, gasfitters, electricians and air conditioning work.

Victoria splits it. The Victorian Building Authority registers builders and licenses plumbers. Energy Safe Victoria licenses electrical workers and registers electrical contractors. Searching the wrong body is the single most common reason someone concludes a legitimate tradie is unlicensed.

Our [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/) points at the right register for the trade and state you pick, and the manual steps are in [how to check a tradie licence](/guides/how-to-check-a-tradie-licence/).

## Five checks before you hire across the border

1. Ask which state the work is in. Not where the business is. Where the job is.
2. Get the licence or registration number and the exact legal entity name on the quote.
3. Search the register for the state where the work will happen, and check the class covers the work.
4. Ask what compliance certificate you will receive when the job is finished, and who issues it.
5. For residential building work over the threshold, ask for the warranty insurance certificate for that state before you pay a deposit.

None of that takes long. All of it is much cheaper than finding out afterwards that the certificate you need does not exist.

## The practical reality on the Murray

Most established trade businesses in the border towns already hold what they need in both states, because half their work is on the other side. It is the newer operators, and businesses coming down from further away for a single job, where the gaps show up.

If a business tells you it is not licensed in the other state but can do the work anyway because of mutual recognition, that answer is incomplete. Ask which arrangement they are relying on, and ask what certificate you will get at the end. A tradie who works both sides regularly will answer both questions without pausing.

For the town by town view of how this plays out day to day, read [hiring a tradie on the border](/guides/hiring-a-tradie-on-the-border/). To start from a listing, try [plumbers in Albury](/nsw/albury/plumbers/) or [electricians in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/electricians/), where the state of each licence is shown on the profile.

faqs.q: Does a NSW licence automatically let a tradie work in Victoria?
faqs.a: Not automatically for every trade. Automatic Mutual Recognition covers many occupations, but some are excluded or were deferred by a state, and notification requirements apply. Check the current position with the regulator for the state where the work will be done before you rely on it.

faqs.q: Which state's rules apply if the tradie is from the other side?
faqs.a: The rules of the state where the work is physically done. A Victorian electrician wiring a house in Albury works to New South Wales requirements. A New South Wales plumber working in Wodonga issues Victorian compliance paperwork.

faqs.q: Is mutual recognition the same as Automatic Mutual Recognition?
faqs.a: No. Mutual recognition means applying for and holding a second licence in the other state. Automatic Mutual Recognition means working in the other state on your home licence without a second one, where the occupation is covered. A business can use either, and many border businesses simply hold both licences.

faqs.q: Where do I complain about work done on the other side of the border?
faqs.a: To the regulator for the state where the work was done. New South Wales work goes to NSW Fair Trading and then NCAT. Victorian work goes to Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Victorian Building Authority and then VCAT. Keep the quote, the invoice and any compliance certificate, because you will be asked for them.

faqs.q: Does a builder's warranty insurance cover jobs in both states?
faqs.a: No. New South Wales home building compensation cover and Victorian domestic building insurance are separate schemes with separate policies. A builder working both sides of the border needs the right cover for each job over the relevant threshold. Ask for the certificate that matches the state the house is in.

title: How to check a tradie licence in NSW and Victoria
description: A step by step check against the NSW Fair Trading, Victorian Building Authority and Energy Safe Victoria registers, in about five minutes.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Checking a licence takes about five minutes and it is the highest value five minutes in the whole hiring process. An unlicensed job can void your insurance, block a sale, and leave you with no access to the statutory warranty schemes. Here is how to do it properly in both states.

## Step 1: get the number, and the exact name

Ask for the licence or registration number and the full legal entity name. Not the trading name on the ute. The name on the quote is what you search for, because a licence is issued to a person or to a company, and those are different records.

If the quote says a trading name only, ask for the ABN as well. You can look an ABN up on the Australian Business Register and see the entity behind it, when it was registered, and whether it is registered for GST. A brand new ABN on a large residential job is not automatically a problem, but it is a reason to ask more questions.

## Step 2: pick the right register

This is where most checks fail before they start.

| Work | State | Register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Builder, plumber, drainer, gasfitter, electrician, air conditioning | NSW | NSW Fair Trading licence check |
| Builder, building surveyor, building inspector | VIC | Victorian Building Authority |
| Plumber, registered plumber | VIC | Victorian Building Authority |
| Electrical worker, electrical contractor | VIC | Energy Safe Victoria |
| Company or business name | Both | ASIC registers |
| ABN and GST status | Both | Australian Business Register |

Searching the Victorian Building Authority for an electrician returns nothing, and plenty of people take that as proof of an unlicensed operator. It is not. Electrical sits with Energy Safe Victoria. Our [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/) sends you to the right one for the trade and state you choose.

## Step 3: match four fields, not one

When the record comes up, check four things.

1. **The name.** Does it match the entity on the quote, exactly?
2. **The status.** Current, expired, suspended or cancelled. Expired means not licensed today.
3. **The class or category.** This is the field people skip and it is the one that matters most.
4. **Conditions.** Some licences carry restrictions, for example supervision requirements or limits on the value or type of work.

A screenshot of a licence card proves nothing. Cards are easy to fake and easy to keep after a licence lapses. The register is the record.

## Step 4: understand what the class means

In New South Wales the distinction that trips people up is between a contractor licence and a certificate. A contractor licence lets a person or company contract directly with you and take your money. A qualified supervisor certificate or a tradesperson certificate lets someone do or supervise the work, but not contract for it in their own name. If the person quoting you holds only a certificate, ask who is actually contracting.

In Victoria, plumbing splits into classes such as water supply, sanitary, drainage, roofing for stormwater, gasfitting, mechanical services, irrigation and fire protection. A licensed plumber can certify their own work in the classes they hold. A registered plumber can carry out work but cannot issue a compliance certificate, so their work has to be signed off by someone who can. Both are legitimate. They are not interchangeable.

In Victorian building, the registration categories separate domestic builder from commercial builder, and separate limited categories such as carpentry or bricklaying from unlimited registration. A carpentry registration does not cover managing a full house build.

## What not licensed for this work looks like

In practice, these are the patterns worth catching.

- The licence is current but the class does not include gasfitting, and the job is a gas cooktop.
- The licence belongs to an individual, and the quote is from a company with a different ABN and no licence of its own.
- The registration is a limited category, such as carpentry, and the job is a full extension with structural work.
- The record shows expired, and the tradie says the renewal is in the post.
- The person is a registered plumber in Victoria and there is no licensed plumber named who will issue the compliance certificate.
- The business is quoting work in the other state and cannot say which mutual recognition arrangement it is relying on. The detail is in [our guide to NSW and Victorian licence rules](/guides/nsw-vic-licence-rules/).

## Step 5: check the paperwork you will receive

A licence check tells you who is entitled to do the work. The certificate at the end tells you the work was done. Ask, before the job starts, what you will be given when it finishes.

For electrical work in Victoria that is a Certificate of Electrical Safety. For plumbing work in Victoria it is a compliance certificate for the classes that require one. In New South Wales, notifiable plumbing work is notified to the regulator and you should receive a certificate of compliance for the work. Building work over the threshold in either state needs the relevant warranty insurance certificate before you pay a deposit.

## If the check comes back bad

Do not argue about it on the phone. Ask them to send the licence number again, because transposed digits are common and the record may simply be under a company name you were not given.

If it is genuinely unlicensed, do not proceed and do not pay a deposit. Report it to NSW Fair Trading or to the Victorian regulator that covers the trade. Unlicensed work is an offence in both states, and the consumer protection schemes that would normally back you up generally do not apply to it.

Every trade listing on LocalsKnow shows the licence number, the issuing state and the date we last checked it. Browse the [builders category](/categories/builders/), or start with [builders in Wagga Wagga](/nsw/wagga-wagga/builders/) or [plumbers in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/plumbers/).

faqs.q: Is a photo of a licence card good enough?
faqs.a: No. Cards are easy to reproduce and stay in the wallet long after a licence expires. Search the public register for the number instead, and check the status and class shown there. The register is the only record that is current.

faqs.q: Why can I not find a Victorian electrician on the VBA register?
faqs.a: Because electrical licensing in Victoria is handled by Energy Safe Victoria, not the Victorian Building Authority. The VBA covers builders, plumbers and building surveyors. Search the right body before concluding anyone is unlicensed.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a contractor licence and a supervisor certificate in NSW?
faqs.a: A contractor licence lets the holder contract with you and take payment for the work. A qualified supervisor certificate lets the holder do or supervise the work under someone else's contractor licence. If your quote comes from a certificate holder with no contractor licence behind it, ask who is legally contracting for the job.

faqs.q: Does an ABN mean a business is licensed?
faqs.a: No. An ABN is a tax registration and anyone can get one. It tells you the legal entity and whether they are registered for GST, which is worth knowing, but it says nothing about trade licensing. Check the trade register separately.

faqs.q: What should I do if work has already been done by an unlicensed tradie?
faqs.a: Stop further payments and report it to NSW Fair Trading or the relevant Victorian regulator. Get the work inspected by a licensed practitioner so you know what has to be rectified. Keep every quote, invoice and message, because that record is what a tribunal will ask for.

faqs.q: How often should a licence be rechecked?
faqs.a: Check it before you sign, and again before a job that runs for months finishes. Licences expire, get suspended and get cancelled during long projects. The date we last verified a listing is shown on every trade profile on this site.

title: Hiring a tradie on the Albury Wodonga border
description: The licence that matters is the one for the state the job is in, not the state the ute is registered in. Here is how that works.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Albury and Wodonga are about six kilometres apart across the Lincoln Causeway. People live on one side and work on the other, shop on one side and play sport on the other. Trade businesses cross the river a dozen times a week. The regulations do not cross with them.

That mismatch is the single most useful thing to understand before you hire anywhere along the Murray. It applies just as much at Corowa and Wahgunyah, Mulwala and Yarrawonga, Tocumwal and Cobram, Moama and Echuca, and Barham and Koondrook.

## The rule in one line

The state where the work is physically done decides which licence, which certificate, which insurance and which tribunal apply.

Not where the business is registered. Not where the ute is registered. Not where the owner sleeps. The address of the job.

A Wodonga electrician rewiring a kitchen in Lavington is doing New South Wales work and must be entitled to do it in New South Wales. An Albury plumber replacing a hot water unit in Baranduda is doing Victorian work and must issue the Victorian compliance paperwork. Both are completely normal arrangements. Both need the right entitlement behind them.

## What that means in practice

For the same job, these things change with the side of the river.

- **The register you search.** New South Wales work is checked against NSW Fair Trading. Victorian building and plumbing work is checked against the Victorian Building Authority. Victorian electrical work is checked against Energy Safe Victoria. The walkthrough is in [how to check a tradie licence](/guides/how-to-check-a-tradie-licence/).
- **The certificate you get at the end.** Victorian electrical work produces a Certificate of Electrical Safety. Victorian plumbing work in the certifying classes produces a compliance certificate. New South Wales notifiable plumbing work is notified in New South Wales.
- **The warranty insurance.** Residential building work over the threshold needs home building compensation cover in New South Wales and domestic building insurance in Victoria. Separate schemes, separate policies, and only the one matching the job's state is any use to you.
- **Where a dispute goes.** New South Wales work leads to NSW Fair Trading and NCAT. Victorian work leads to Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Victorian Building Authority and VCAT.

The mechanics of how a licence does and does not travel are set out in [our guide to NSW and Victorian licence rules](/guides/nsw-vic-licence-rules/).

## The questions that sort it out in two minutes

When a business quotes a job on the other side of the river, ask three things.

1. Are you licensed or registered in the state this job is in, and what is the number?
2. What certificate or paperwork will I receive when the work is finished?
3. If this is residential building work over the threshold, which state's warranty insurance policy covers it?

An established border business answers all three without hesitation, because it deals with this every week. Hesitation on question two is the one to pay attention to.

## Travel charges and the causeway

Crossing the river costs the tradie almost nothing in distance. Albury to Wodonga is a shorter run than Albury to Thurgoona at peak hour. Some businesses still apply an interstate travel charge out of habit, which is worth questioning when the job is 15 minutes from the depot.

The genuine travel cost appears further out. Wodonga to Culcairn, Corowa to Rutherglen or Yarrawonga to Deniliquin are real distances and a fair quote will price them. Ask for the travel component as a separate line so you can see what you are paying for, either as a kilometre rate or a named zone fee.

## Two things that are the same, and one that is not

Both states run on the same clock. New South Wales and Victoria share Australian Eastern Standard Time and both observe daylight saving on the same dates, so a 7am start means the same thing on both sides. The exception in New South Wales is Broken Hill, which runs on central time, and that is a long way from the Murray.

Building standards are largely shared too. Both states apply the National Construction Code, and the plumbing and wiring standards are national documents. The differences are in licensing, certification and insurance rather than in how the pipe is laid.

The thing that is not the same is the calendar. Victoria gazettes Melbourne Cup Day and the Friday before the AFL Grand Final. New South Wales does not. Labour Day falls in March in Victoria and October in New South Wales. That drives callout loadings on days when the town across the river is working normally, which we cover in [the public holidays comparison](/guides/public-holidays-nsw-vs-vic/).

## Insurance, warranty and the long tail

Think about who you will ring in two years, not just who is cheapest this week. A business that works both sides regularly, holds the entitlements for both, and has a depot within half an hour is worth a premium over an operator who came up from Melbourne for one job.

Check that public liability cover is current and that it does not exclude work in the other state. It rarely does, but the certificate takes ten seconds to read and it names the insured entity, which is another way of confirming who you are actually dealing with.

For anything structural, confirm the warranty insurance before you pay a deposit. That is the protection that survives if the business folds, and it only exists for the state the house is in.

## Where to start looking

LocalsKnow models service area separately from the physical address, so a Wodonga business that services Albury appears on both towns' pages with its licences shown for each state. Start with [plumbers in Albury](/nsw/albury/plumbers/), [electricians in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/electricians/), or run a number through the [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/) before you call.

faqs.q: Can a Wodonga tradie legally work in Albury?
faqs.a: Yes, provided they are entitled to do that work in New South Wales, either by holding a New South Wales licence or through Automatic Mutual Recognition where it covers their occupation. The job also has to meet New South Wales requirements for notification and certification. Ask for the number and check it on the NSW Fair Trading register.

faqs.q: Which state's warranty insurance applies to a house on the border?
faqs.a: The state the house is in. A home in Albury needs New South Wales home building compensation cover for building work over the threshold, and a home in Wodonga needs Victorian domestic building insurance. Get the certificate that matches the property address before paying a deposit.

faqs.q: Is there a time difference between Albury and Wodonga?
faqs.a: No. New South Wales and Victoria share the same time zone and observe daylight saving on the same dates, so appointment times are identical on both sides. The only New South Wales exception is Broken Hill, which runs on central time.

faqs.q: Should I expect an interstate travel charge for a job across the causeway?
faqs.a: Not for a routine Albury to Wodonga job, which is a shorter trip than many jobs within either town. Genuine travel charges apply further out, for example to Corowa, Culcairn or Yarrawonga. Ask for travel to be listed as its own line on the quote.

faqs.q: Where do I take a dispute about work done across the border?
faqs.a: To the regulator and tribunal for the state where the work was done. New South Wales work goes to NSW Fair Trading and then NCAT. Victorian work goes to Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Victorian Building Authority and then VCAT.

title: What a pre purchase building inspection costs
description: Indicative $400 to $800 for a house inspection in regional NSW and VIC, plus what the report does not cover and when to book it.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
A pre purchase inspection is the cheapest insurance in the whole buying process, and the one most often skipped because the auction is on Saturday. The ranges below are indicative for regional New South Wales and Victoria. City pricing is different and so is the competition for inspectors.

## Indicative costs

| Inspection | Indicative range |
| --- | --- |
| Standard house, pre purchase building report | $400 to $700 |
| Timber pest inspection on its own | $250 to $450 |
| Building and pest combined | $500 to $900 |
| Acreage, large or two storey homes | add $100 to $300 |
| Travel beyond the inspector's base town | add $80 to $250 |
| Structural engineer's report | $600 to $1,800 |
| Asbestos identification and sampling | $400 to $1,200 |
| Strata or owners corporation records search | $250 to $500 |

Combined building and pest is usually cheaper than booking the two separately, because it is one trip and one set of ladders. In towns like Mudgee, Bright or Deniliquin there may be only a handful of inspectors, so the travel line matters and the lead time matters more.

## What the standard report actually is

A pre purchase building inspection in Australia is generally carried out to Australian Standard 4349.1, and a timber pest inspection to AS 4349.3. Both are visual and non invasive. The inspector looks at what can be safely accessed and does not cut open walls, lift fixed floor coverings or move stored goods.

That scope is why the report has a long list of areas not inspected. Subfloors too tight to enter, roof spaces with no access hatch, and anything behind a full garage of boxes will be excluded. Read that list first. It tells you what you still do not know.

The report should describe the condition of the structure, the roof, the wet areas, the drainage away from the house, and any major defect or safety hazard. It is not a valuation, it is not a compliance audit of the wiring or the plumbing, and it does not certify that past work was approved.

## What it will not tell you

Three gaps catch buyers regularly.

The first is unapproved work. An inspector may note that the pergola or the enclosed carport looks like an addition, but confirming approval means checking with the council. On regional blocks, unapproved sheds, decks and second dwellings are common and they become your problem at settlement.

The second is the septic system. A building report does not assess an onsite wastewater system. If the property is unsewered, and most rural blocks in the Riverina, Ovens Murray and the Goulburn Valley are, you want that looked at separately. The rules and costs are in [our septic and onsite wastewater guide](/guides/septic-and-onsite-wastewater-rules/).

The third is the electrical and plumbing condition beyond what is visible. An old switchboard with rewireable fuses gets a note. Whether the circuits are safe needs a licensed electrician. Ask for a quote from [an electrician](/categories/electricians/) if the report flags the board.

## Timber pests in inland NSW and Victoria

Termites are a live risk across most of inland New South Wales and northern Victoria, and it does not follow the price of the house. Older homes on stumps, houses with garden beds built up against weatherboards, and blocks with old stumps or buried timber are the usual candidates.

A pest report will note conducive conditions as well as active activity. Conducive conditions matter, because they are what turns a clean report today into damage in five years. Poor subfloor ventilation and soil levels above the damp course are the two most common findings in older regional housing and both are fixable.

If the report finds activity, get a treatment quote before you make an offer, not after. Treatment cost varies enormously with construction type. Browse [pest control](/categories/pest-control/) listings for your town.

## Timing, cooling off and auctions

In New South Wales, a private treaty purchase generally carries a cooling off period of a few business days with a small forfeit if you withdraw, and there is no cooling off period on an auction purchase. Victoria also provides a short cooling off period on private sales, with a penalty, and none at auction. The exact periods and penalty amounts are set in each state's legislation and have been adjusted over time, so confirm the current position with your conveyancer or solicitor before you rely on it.

The practical consequence is the same in both states. If you are bidding at auction, the inspection has to happen before the hammer falls. Inspectors in regional towns book out one to two weeks ahead in a busy market, so ring them the day the property is listed.

## Choosing the inspector

Ask who is doing the inspection and what they are qualified in. In Victoria, building inspectors are a registered class with the Victorian Building Authority. In New South Wales, pre purchase inspections are commonly done by licensed builders or by consultants who hold building licences and pest technician qualifications.

Then ask four things.

1. Do you carry professional indemnity insurance, and can I see the certificate?
2. Can I see a sample report from a similar property?
3. Can I walk through with you at the end, or will you take my call to explain the findings?
4. Do you have any relationship with the agent or the vendor?

The last one matters. The report should be commissioned by you and written for you. A report supplied by the vendor is not worthless, but you did not choose the inspector and you are not the client.

A short verbal debrief is often more useful than the document. A good inspector will tell you plainly which items are cosmetic, which are a negotiating point and which are a walk away.

## Using the report

A report that finds problems is a report doing its job. Use it to price the fix, then decide whether to renegotiate, ask for the work to be completed before settlement, or withdraw.

Get real quotes for the major items rather than guessing. Start with [builders in Albury](/nsw/albury/builders/) or [builders in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/builders/), and check any licence you are given with the [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/).

faqs.q: How much does a building and pest inspection cost in regional NSW or Victoria?
faqs.a: An indicative range for a standard house is $500 to $900 for a combined building and pest inspection, or $400 to $700 for the building report alone. Acreage, two storey homes and travel outside the inspector's base town add to that. Ranges are indicative and vary by town and inspector.

faqs.q: Does a building inspection cover the septic system?
faqs.a: No. A standard pre purchase inspection under AS 4349.1 does not assess onsite wastewater systems. If the property is unsewered, arrange a separate inspection of the tank, the treatment unit and the land application area. A failing system is one of the most expensive surprises on a rural block.

faqs.q: Can I get an inspection before an auction?
faqs.a: Yes, and you must, because auction purchases carry no cooling off period in either state. Book as soon as the property is listed, since regional inspectors are often a week or two ahead. Arrange access through the agent for the same time as an open inspection if the vendor prefers.

faqs.q: What does the inspector not look at?
faqs.a: Anything not safely accessible or visible, including areas behind walls, under fixed floor coverings, inside inaccessible subfloors and roof spaces, and behind stored goods. Every report lists these exclusions. Read that section first, because it defines what the report cannot tell you.

faqs.q: Should I use the report the agent gives me?
faqs.a: Treat it as background, not as your own advice. You did not choose the inspector, and the report was commissioned by someone whose interest is the sale. Commission your own inspection if the purchase matters, and ask the inspector directly whether they have any relationship with the agent or vendor.

faqs.q: Is a defect report the same as a pre purchase inspection?
faqs.a: No. A pre purchase inspection gives a general overview of the property's condition to a standard scope. A defect report investigates a specific problem, such as cracking or water ingress, and often needs a structural engineer. If the pre purchase report flags something serious, the engineer's report is the next step.

title: Public holidays: NSW and Victoria compared
description: Melbourne Cup Day, Grand Final Friday, Labour Day and the August bank holiday all differ. Here is what that does to callout rates.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
If you live on the Murray you already know the feeling. The shops are shut on one side of the river and open on the other, and nobody warned you. Public holidays are declared by each state, so New South Wales and Victoria do not keep the same calendar.

This matters for two reasons. It changes when you can get a trade, a delivery or a council office, and it changes what an emergency callout costs.

**All dates are set annually by each state government and some are moved or substituted from year to year. Check the official New South Wales Government public holidays page and the Business Victoria public holidays page for the current year before you plan anything around them.**

## The days both states share

New Year's Day, Australia Day, Good Friday, Easter Saturday, Easter Sunday, Easter Monday, Anzac Day, the June holiday for the monarch's birthday, Christmas Day and Boxing Day are gazetted in both states. When Christmas Day, Boxing Day, New Year's Day or Australia Day falls on a weekend, an additional day is usually declared, and the substitution rules are not identical between the states.

## The days that differ

### Labour Day

Victoria takes Labour Day in March. New South Wales takes it in October. Same holiday, different season, seven months apart. This is the difference that surprises people most, because it hits two long weekends a year and neither one lines up.

### Melbourne Cup Day

The first Tuesday in November is a public holiday in Victoria. It is an ordinary working Tuesday in New South Wales. In parts of regional Victoria, councils can arrange for an alternative local day to be gazetted instead, often tied to a local show or festival, so the Cup Day holiday is not universal across the state. Check with the council in your shire.

### The Friday before the AFL Grand Final

Victoria gazettes a public holiday on the Friday before the AFL Grand Final. The date moves with the football calendar and is declared each year. New South Wales has nothing equivalent. For border towns this is the biggest practical difference in the year, because Wodonga trades are on holiday rates while Albury trades are working a normal Friday.

### The August bank holiday

New South Wales has a bank holiday on the first Monday in August. It is not a general public holiday. It applies to banks and some financial institutions, so most workplaces, shops and trades operate normally. Victoria has no equivalent day.

### Local show days and regional variations

Both states allow local public holidays or part day holidays to be declared for particular districts, usually for a show or a race meeting. These are gazetted and they are genuinely local. If a job is booked in a smaller town, it is worth asking whether the local show day is coming up.

## What the difference costs you

Most trade businesses price a public holiday callout at roughly double the weekday rate, often with a minimum of two to four hours and a higher callout fee. That is not regulated, it is commercial practice, and the numbers are indicative rather than fixed.

The cross border consequence is direct. On Melbourne Cup Day, a Wodonga plumber is on holiday rates while an Albury plumber is on a normal Tuesday. On the New South Wales October long weekend, the reverse is true. If your job is not urgent and you can choose which side of the river to call, you can genuinely save money by knowing which state is on holiday.

The base rates that the loading applies to are set out in [what plumbers charge in regional NSW](/guides/what-plumbers-charge-nsw/) and [what electricians charge in regional Victoria](/guides/what-electricians-charge-vic/).

## Beyond callout rates

Several other things follow the state calendar.

- **Council offices and inspections.** A permit or an inspection booked with Albury City is not affected by a Victorian holiday, and a Wodonga inspection is not affected by a New South Wales one. Long weekends that differ by state routinely add a week to approvals.
- **Deliveries and trade suppliers.** A Victorian supplier is shut on Grand Final Friday. If your job depends on parts arriving that day, it does not matter that your side of the river is working.
- **Retail and pub trading.** Trading restrictions on days such as Anzac Day morning and Good Friday are set by each state and differ in detail.
- **Penalty rates for staff.** Employers with workers on both sides of the border deal with two calendars in one payroll. There is more on cross border operating in [starting a business in regional NSW or VIC](/guides/starting-a-business-in-regional-nsw-or-vic/).

## Planning around it

Book non urgent work away from either state's long weekends. The fortnight around a shared holiday period is when every trade is booked and every response time blows out.

If the work is urgent, ask for the holiday rate in writing before the tradie is dispatched. A genuine emergency, meaning a burst pipe, no power, a gas leak or a security issue, is worth the loading. A dripping tap on Melbourne Cup Day is not.

If you are travelling, check accommodation early. Grand Final Friday and the Cup weekend fill motels across north east Victoria and the border towns, and cancellation terms tighten on those dates. That is covered in [what to ask before you book a motel](/guides/what-to-ask-before-you-book-a-motel/).

To find someone working today, the listings for [plumbers in Albury](/nsw/albury/plumbers/) and [electricians in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/electricians/) show trading hours with each state's holiday calendar applied.

faqs.q: Is Melbourne Cup Day a public holiday in New South Wales?
faqs.a: No. Melbourne Cup Day is a Victorian public holiday on the first Tuesday in November and an ordinary working day in New South Wales. Some regional Victorian councils substitute an alternative local day instead, so check with your council. Confirm the current year's date on the Business Victoria public holidays page.

faqs.q: Does New South Wales have a Grand Final Friday holiday?
faqs.a: No. The public holiday on the Friday before the AFL Grand Final applies in Victoria only, and the date is declared each year with the football calendar. Border businesses in Wodonga will be on holiday rates while Albury businesses work normally.

faqs.q: When is Labour Day in each state?
faqs.a: Victoria takes Labour Day in March and New South Wales takes it in October. The two long weekends do not overlap. Check the official state pages for the exact dates each year.

faqs.q: What is the New South Wales bank holiday in August?
faqs.a: It is a limited holiday on the first Monday in August that applies to banks and some financial institutions, not a general public holiday. Shops, trades and most workplaces operate as normal. Victoria has no equivalent day.

faqs.q: How much more does a public holiday callout cost?
faqs.a: Around double the standard weekday rate is common, with a higher callout fee and a minimum of two to four hours. These are indicative commercial rates, not regulated ones, and they vary between businesses. Ask for the holiday rate in writing before the tradie is dispatched.

title: Choosing a removalist in regional NSW and Victoria
description: Albury to Wodonga is an interstate move at six kilometres. What a binding quote covers, and where transit insurance stops.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
A move from Albury to Wodonga is an interstate move. It is also six kilometres. That sentence explains most of the confusion people have when they start ringing removalists on the border, because the word interstate triggers different pricing, different insurance wording and sometimes a different truck.

## Interstate and intrastate, and why the label matters

Intrastate means the move stays inside one state. Wagga Wagga to Albury is intrastate. Bendigo to Shepparton is intrastate. Most removalists price these by the hour with a crew and a truck.

Interstate means the move crosses a state border, no matter how short the trip. Albury to Wodonga, Moama to Echuca and Mulwala to Yarrawonga are all interstate. Long distance interstate moves are usually priced on volume in cubic metres, sometimes with backloading, and the transit insurance wording is often different.

For short border hops, most local operators will quote hourly anyway. If a business quotes you a long distance interstate rate to cross the causeway, get another quote.

## How removalists price

**Hourly.** Two movers and a truck in regional New South Wales and Victoria sit in an indicative range of $120 to $190 an hour including GST, with three movers higher. Expect a minimum of three or four hours, and check whether the clock starts at the depot or at your front door.

**Fixed or binding quote.** The removalist inspects the house, in person or by video walkthrough, and commits to a price for the inventory they have seen. This is the better structure for anything long distance.

**Volume based.** Long distance moves priced per cubic metre, sometimes shared with other loads. Cheaper, slower, and the delivery window is a range of days rather than a time.

Indicative totals help calibrate. A three bedroom house moving within a regional town commonly lands between $900 and $2,200. Albury to Melbourne or Wagga Wagga to Sydney for the same house commonly lands between $2,200 and $5,000 depending on volume, access and timing.

## What a binding quote actually binds

A binding quote is only binding on the inventory and the access described in it. Add a shed full of tools on the day, or fail to mention the piano, and the price changes legitimately.

A binding quote should name the inventory, the access at both ends, the date, the crew size, the truck size, what is included in the hourly rate or fixed price, and every additional charge that can apply.

The usual extras are stairs, a long carry from the truck to the door, a shuttle vehicle when a semi cannot reach the property, a heavy item fee for pianos, safes and pool tables, packing materials, dismantling and reassembly, and waiting time. Ask for that list up front. A removalist who will not put the extras in writing is quoting a number that is not real.

Rural access is the biggest single cause of a blown out quote in this part of the country. A wet dirt driveway, a low gateway, an unbridged creek crossing or a house 400 metres from the nearest hard stand all mean a shuttle or a longer carry. Tell them before the day.

## Insurance, and the words that matter

This is where most disputes start. There are three separate things and people assume they are one.

1. **Public liability.** Covers damage to property and injury to people. Every legitimate operator carries it. It does not cover your furniture.
2. **Carrier's liability or goods in transit.** Covers the load in limited circumstances, often only where the vehicle is involved in a collision, overturns, catches fire or is stolen. A scratched sideboard carried down a hallway is usually not covered.
3. **Full accidental damage or transit insurance.** Broader cover, usually an optional extra bought as a percentage of the declared value of your goods.

Read the exclusions. Owner packed cartons are commonly excluded from cover for breakage, which is exactly why the removalist offers to pack your glassware. Items of unusual value normally need to be declared and listed separately. Cover often stops if goods go into storage under a different arrangement.

Ask for the certificate of currency and the policy summary before you book, and check the excess. An excess of $500 on a policy protecting a $6,000 inventory changes the value of the cover considerably.

## Checks before you book

1. Look up the ABN and confirm the trading entity matches the quote. Our [guide to starting a business in regional NSW or VIC](/guides/starting-a-business-in-regional-nsw-or-vic/) explains what an ABN record shows.
2. Ask whether they are a member of an industry body such as the Australian Furniture Removers Association, which sets a code of conduct and a dispute process.
3. Confirm the crew are employees or contractors of that business, not a labour hire crew unknown to them.
4. Get the cancellation and rescheduling terms in writing, including what happens if you settle late.
5. Confirm the payment terms. Payment before unload is common practice for interstate work and is worth knowing in advance rather than at the kerb.
6. Confirm the deposit, and never pay a large deposit in cash to an operator you cannot verify.

## Timing in the country

Regional demand is seasonal in a way city demand is not. School holidays, the end of the financial year, harvest, and the fortnight around Christmas book out the good crews early. Settlement dates that land on a Friday are the hardest to fill, because everyone wants the same day.

Book four to six weeks ahead where you can. If your settlement date is not certain, ask what the reschedule policy is before you pay a deposit, because in regional towns there is often only one crew available and moving your date can mean moving to the back of the queue.

Finally, check the truck size against the driveway and the street. In older parts of Albury, Bendigo and Wagga Wagga, a semi trailer simply cannot get in, and finding that out on the morning costs you a shuttle fee.

Start with the listings for [removalists](/categories/removalists/), or the local pages for [Albury](/nsw/albury/removalists/) and [Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/removalists/).

faqs.q: Is Albury to Wodonga an interstate move?
faqs.a: Yes, technically it crosses the New South Wales and Victorian border, even though it is about six kilometres. Most local removalists still quote it as an ordinary hourly local job. If a business applies long distance interstate pricing to a causeway move, get a second quote.

faqs.q: What is a binding quote?
faqs.a: It is a fixed price for a specified inventory and specified access, given after the removalist has inspected the house in person or by video. It stays fixed unless what you are moving or the access changes. Ask for the list of additional charges that can still apply, because stairs, long carries and shuttle vehicles usually sit outside it.

faqs.q: Does removalist insurance cover everything in the truck?
faqs.a: Usually not. Carrier's liability often only responds when the vehicle collides, overturns, catches fire or is stolen, and it does not cover general handling damage. Full accidental damage cover is an optional extra priced on the declared value of your goods. Owner packed cartons are commonly excluded, so read the exclusions before you pack.

faqs.q: How far ahead should I book a removalist in a regional town?
faqs.a: Four to six weeks is sensible, and longer around Christmas, school holidays and the end of the financial year. Regional towns often have only a handful of crews, so rescheduling can push you back weeks. Confirm the reschedule policy before paying a deposit if your settlement date is not locked in.

faqs.q: Why is there a shuttle fee for a rural property?
faqs.a: Because a large truck cannot always reach the house. Narrow gates, soft dirt driveways, low branches and tight bends mean the load has to be transferred to a smaller vehicle and driven in. Describe the access when you get the quote and the fee will be in the price rather than a surprise on the day.

title: Septic and onsite wastewater rules in NSW and Victoria
description: Council approval, permits to install, land capability assessments, and indicative costs from $8,000 to $25,000 for a new system.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Anywhere off the sewer, the wastewater system is a regulated piece of infrastructure, not a plumbing detail. Most of the rural Riverina, the Murray shires, Ovens Murray and the Goulburn Valley run on septic tanks or aerated treatment systems, and the rules are stricter than most people assume.

Two permissions matter. Approval to install or alter a system, and approval to operate it once it is in. Doing the work first and asking later is how people end up ripping out a $20,000 installation.

## New South Wales

In New South Wales, onsite sewage management is regulated by councils under the Local Government Act. You need council approval to install or alter a sewage management facility, and a separate approval to operate it, which is generally renewed on a cycle set by the council.

The treatment unit itself has to be an accredited model. NSW Health accredits domestic wastewater treatment systems, and a council will not approve an unaccredited unit. Ask the supplier for the accreditation, not just the brochure.

The application usually needs a site plan, the soil and site assessment that sizes the land application area, the accreditation details of the unit, and the licence details of whoever is installing it. Councils in the Riverina and the Murray shires publish their own checklists and they vary, so ring the environmental health officer before you design anything.

## Victoria

In Victoria, onsite wastewater systems handling less than 5,000 litres a day are approved by the local council under the framework set by the Environment Protection Authority. The council issues a permit to install or alter a septic tank system, and a permit to use it once the work is inspected.

The treatment system must hold an EPA Certificate of Conformity. That certificate names the conditions the system is approved for, and the council will check it.

Most Victorian councils require a Land Capability Assessment for new systems and for many alterations. That is a report by a suitably qualified consultant on whether the site can absorb and treat the effluent, taking in soil type, slope, setbacks, groundwater, flooding and the size of the block. It drives the whole design. On tight blocks it sometimes concludes the site cannot support the system the owner wanted.

The Victorian code of practice for onsite wastewater management sets the technical rules, and the plumbing work follows the national standard for onsite domestic wastewater management.

## Who can do the work

Installation is licensed plumbing work in both states. In New South Wales it needs a drainer with the appropriate licence from NSW Fair Trading. In Victoria it needs a licensed plumber holding the drainage class and, where relevant, sanitary and water, registered with the Victorian Building Authority. Victorian work in a certifying class produces a compliance certificate at the end.

Earthworks, tank delivery and trenching are often done by a separate contractor working under the plumber. That is fine, as long as the licensed person is responsible for the installation and issues the paperwork. Check the number before the excavator arrives, using [our licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/) or the steps in [how to check a tradie licence](/guides/how-to-check-a-tradie-licence/).

Electrical connection for an aerated system, meaning the blower, the pump and the alarm, is electrical work and needs a licensed electrician. In Victoria that produces a Certificate of Electrical Safety.

## Indicative costs

| Item | Indicative range |
| --- | --- |
| Land capability assessment or soil and site report | $800 to $2,200 |
| Council permit to install | a few hundred dollars, varies by council |
| Conventional septic tank with absorption trenches, installed | $8,000 to $18,000 |
| Aerated wastewater treatment system, installed | $12,000 to $28,000 |
| Sand filter or advanced system on a difficult site | $18,000 to $40,000 |
| Pump out of a full tank | $300 to $700 |
| Mandatory service visits on an aerated system, per year | $250 to $600 |

Permit fees are set by each council and change, so get the current figure from the council rather than an old forum post. Everything above is indicative, and a difficult site changes it substantially. Rock, high groundwater, a steep fall, a small block or a flood prone river frontage all push the design up a tier.

## The ongoing obligations

An aerated system is not fit and forget. Most approvals require a service contract with scheduled visits, and the service reports go to the council. Skipping servicing is the most common breach, and it is also how a system quietly fails until the effluent surfaces in the paddock.

A conventional septic tank needs pumping out on a cycle that depends on tank size and household size. The land application area needs to stay clear of vehicles, stock and hard surfaces, and it needs to keep its vegetation, because the plants do a good share of the work.

Do not divert stormwater into the trenches, and keep wipes, fats and heavy disinfectants out of the system. Those three habits account for most of the failures a service technician sees.

## Buying a property with a septic system

A standard pre purchase building inspection does not assess wastewater. Arrange a separate inspection, and ask the vendor for the approval to install, the approval or permit to use, and the service records. Councils hold records of approved systems, and a system with no record is a genuine problem to price in.

The questions worth asking are simple. When was it installed, what type is it, when was it last pumped out or serviced, where is the land application area, and has it ever surfaced or smelled after heavy rain. Ask the neighbours the last one. There is more on inspection scope in [what a building inspection costs](/guides/what-a-building-inspection-costs/).

If the system is failing, replacement is not a small job, and on a constrained block the council may require a higher grade system than the one being replaced. That is a negotiating point before contracts, not a surprise afterwards.

## Where to start

Ring the council first. In both states the environmental health officer will tell you what the local requirements are, and the good ones will tell you what usually gets knocked back before you spend money on a design.

Then get quotes from installers who work in that shire regularly, because they know the local checklists. Browse [septic services](/categories/septic-services/), or start with local listings for [plumbers in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/plumbers/).

faqs.q: Do I need council approval to replace a septic tank?
faqs.a: Yes, in both states. New South Wales requires council approval to install or alter a sewage management facility, and Victoria requires a council permit to install or alter a septic tank system. Replacing a failed system is an alteration, so the approval process applies even when nothing else on the property changes.

faqs.q: What is a Land Capability Assessment?
faqs.a: It is a report on whether a site can treat and absorb the wastewater a household will produce, based on soil, slope, setbacks, groundwater and block size. Most Victorian councils require one for new onsite systems, and New South Wales councils require an equivalent soil and site assessment. It sets the size and type of the land application area, so it comes before the design, not after.

faqs.q: How much does a new onsite wastewater system cost?
faqs.a: An indicative range is $8,000 to $18,000 for a conventional septic tank with absorption trenches, and $12,000 to $28,000 for an aerated treatment system, installed. Difficult sites with rock, steep falls or high groundwater cost more again. Add the assessment report and the council permit fee, which each council sets separately.

faqs.q: Who is allowed to install a septic system?
faqs.a: A licensed drainer or plumber holding the right class for the state where the work is done. In New South Wales that is a licence from NSW Fair Trading, and in Victoria it is a licensed plumber registered with the Victorian Building Authority who can issue a compliance certificate. Excavation contractors can do the earthworks, but the licensed person is responsible for the installation.

faqs.q: How often does an aerated system need servicing?
faqs.a: Most approvals require scheduled servicing on a set cycle, commonly quarterly, under a contract with a technician who reports to the council. Missing services is the most common breach of an approval to operate. Budget an indicative $250 to $600 a year plus repairs.

faqs.q: Can I install a septic system myself?
faqs.a: No. Installation is licensed plumbing and drainage work in both states, and the system must be an approved or accredited model installed to the approval conditions. Unapproved work can be ordered out at the owner's cost and will surface in any future sale.

title: Solar incentives in NSW and Victoria, explained plainly
description: How the federal certificate scheme discounts a system, what Solar Victoria runs, and why you should never trust a quoted rebate figure.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Solar support in Australia comes from two directions. A federal scheme that discounts almost every eligible system, and state programs that come and go. The federal part is stable enough to explain. The state part changes often enough that any dollar figure printed here would be wrong within months.

So this guide explains the machinery. For the numbers, go to the current program page. Every one of these programs publishes its own eligibility and amounts, and those are the only figures worth relying on.

## The federal certificate scheme

The Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme is the reason a solar quote already looks discounted before any state program is mentioned. It is administered by the Clean Energy Regulator.

How it works. An eligible small system creates small-scale technology certificates, usually called STCs, based on how much electricity it is deemed to generate over the remaining years of the scheme. The certificates have a market value. In practice you assign them to the installer or retailer, and they take the value off your invoice. That is why quotes talk about the price after STCs.

Three consequences follow.

1. It is a point of sale discount, not a cash payment. You do not receive money later.
2. The number of certificates falls each year, because the deeming period shortens as the scheme runs down towards its legislated end. A system installed next year creates fewer certificates than the same system this year.
3. The value of a certificate moves with the market. Two quotes prepared weeks apart can show different discounts for identical hardware.

Eligibility conditions apply, including the requirement that the system is installed and designed by an accredited installer under the scheme, using approved components. The body running installer accreditation has changed in recent years, so ask the installer to name their current accreditation and check it. Batteries were brought into the federal arrangements more recently, and the terms of that support have their own eligibility rules. Check the Clean Energy Regulator's current page.

## Victoria

Victoria runs its household support through Solar Victoria, the state body set up for that purpose. Over the years the Solar Homes program has offered rebates and interest free loans across rooftop solar, solar hot water and batteries, with eligibility tests that have included household income, property value, whether the property is owner occupied or rented, and whether the address has claimed before.

The amounts, the eligibility tests and which technologies are covered have all changed several times. Some streams have closed and reopened. Do not budget from a figure someone quoted you last year and do not budget from a figure in a sales brochure. Check the Solar Victoria site for the current program before you sign anything.

One mechanical detail matters. Where a state rebate applies, the process usually requires an eligibility application and an approval before installation, and it requires the installer to be on the program's approved list. Signing a contract first can disqualify you.

## New South Wales

New South Wales has not run a broad rooftop solar rebate for owner occupiers in the way Victoria has. Instead it delivers incentives through schemes that work at the industry level, including the Peak Demand Reduction Scheme and the Energy Savings Scheme, which create discounts delivered by accredited providers on things such as batteries and efficient appliances.

The practical effect for a household is a discount offered by a participating supplier rather than a rebate you apply for yourself. Programs targeted at low income households and at social housing have also run at various times.

Because these are delivered through providers, the offer you see depends on which provider you talk to. Get more than one quote and ask each of them to identify the scheme the discount comes from. Check the current position on the New South Wales Government energy pages.

## Feed in tariffs

What you get paid for exported power is separate from any rebate and it is not fixed.

In Victoria, minimum feed in tariff arrangements have been set by the Essential Services Commission and the framework has been under review, so the current position needs checking. In New South Wales there is no mandated minimum. IPART publishes an annual benchmark range as guidance, and retailers set their own rates.

Either way, retailer offers vary widely and a high feed in rate is often paired with a higher daily supply charge. Compare the whole plan, not the export rate on its own. For most households now, self consumption is worth more than export.

## Grid connection in the regions

Before anything is installed, the system needs approval from the network distributor. In most of regional New South Wales that is Essential Energy. In north east Victoria it is generally AusNet, and in western Victoria it is generally Powercor.

Distributors commonly limit how much you can export, and the limit depends on the local network, the phase configuration and sometimes the specific feeder. Rural areas with single wire earth return supply have tighter limits again. A good installer handles the application and tells you the export limit before you sign. A bad one installs a large system and tells you afterwards that most of it cannot export.

## How to not get burnt

- Get three written quotes with the panel and inverter make and model on each, not just a total kilowatt figure.
- Ask which scheme every discount comes from and whether it is the federal certificate discount, a state program, or a retailer offer.
- Confirm the installer's accreditation and the electrical licence of the person doing the work. Run it through the [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/), and read [how to check a tradie licence](/guides/how-to-check-a-tradie-licence/) if you want the steps.
